args.rationale: 38-year-old woman with probable primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) from tuberculous adrenalitis. Obtained evidence: calcified bilateral adrenal nodules and old lung/pleural TB lesions on CT (imaging_007); mild darkening of the finger joints and knees (hpi_001, physical_exam_003); a chest opacity five years ago that was never treated for TB and no glucocorticoid use (pmh_002). Hydrocortisone replacement is ordered. No crisis features were documented: no fever and vital signs were not reported. She is admitted to the ward rather than discharged or sent to the ICU for three reasons. First, the adrenal insufficiency has not been confirmed: cortisol, ACTH, electrolytes, renin/aldosterone and the ACTH stimulation test were all unavailable. Second, she needs monitored start of steroid (and possibly fludrocortisone) replacement. Third, she needs a work-up for active TB before any decision on anti-TB therapy. Allergies, current medications, liver function and pregnancy status are still unknown and are safety constraints.
args.followup_or_handoff: 1) Draw baseline 8am cortisol, ACTH, renin, aldosterone, electrolytes, glucose, creatinine and CBC before the first hydrocortisone dose if possible. If a 250 mcg ACTH stimulation test is still needed after steroids have started, hold hydrocortisone for about 24 hours under monitoring or bridge with dexamethasone. 2) Watch for adrenal crisis (low blood pressure, low sodium, high potassium, low glucose, vomiting). If it happens, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus and IV normal saline. 3) Once renin is high or sodium/potassium are abnormal, add fludrocortisone 0.05–0.1 mg daily. 4) TB work-up: IGRA, sputum AFB smear, culture and Xpert x3, and consider chest CT review with infectious disease. If active or adrenal TB is supported, start standard anti-TB therapy. Rifampicin speeds hydrocortisone breakdown, so the hydrocortisone dose will need to be about doubled. 5) Before any anti-TB drugs, confirm allergies, current medications, liver tests, HIV status and pregnancy test. 6) Consult endocrinology. Teach stress dosing and sick-day rules, and provide a medical alert ID and an emergency injectable hydrocortisone kit. 7) After discharge, arrange endocrinology and TB clinic follow-up within 1–2 weeks.
